"Slide one: Supplier Risk Review for Trellis Research Computing," Vikram Salian announced, clicking through the presentation. "As some of you know, Trellis has been our primary cloud provider for the research office’s high-performance computing needs. But their service level agreements have been consistently missed over the past six months."

The room murmured in agreement. Meera Iyengar, the IT project manager, chimed in, "Their last outage took down the medical annex’s data processing for nearly 12 hours. The research office had to delay a critical study because of it."

Vikram nodded. "Exactly. Slide two shows the incident timeline. Notice the uptick in outages starting in Q2. We’ve logged 14 incidents in that period alone, with an average resolution time of 4.2 hours. That’s well above our agreed SLA of 2 hours."

"What’s their explanation?" asked Rohan Deshpande, the IT security lead.

"They blame it on infrastructure upgrades," Vikram replied. "But their communication has been poor. We only found out about the last outage through user complaints, not their monitoring alerts. Slide three outlines our risk assessment: high impact, high likelihood, and high severity. This is a red flag."

Meera crossed her arms. "So what’s the plan? Do we start looking for alternatives?"

Vikram flipped to the next slide. "Yes, but first, we need to formalize this in the supplier risk review. We’ll present our findings to procurement and recommend either renegotiating the SLA or transitioning to a backup provider. I’ve already reached out to two other vendors for quotes."

Rohan added, "We should also document this for the next audit. If Trellis doesn’t improve, we’ll need to justify our decision to switch providers, and having a paper trail will help."

Vikram concluded, "Agreed. Let’s finalize the report by the end of the week and schedule a follow-up with procurement. The research office can’t afford another delay." The team nodded, the urgency of the situation clear.

"Slide one: *Remote Work Stipend Policy – Research Office Perspectives*," Meera Iyengar announced, clicking through her presentation. The room was packed with department heads, their attention fixed on the projector screen. "As some of you know, the research office has been fielding concerns from faculty about the adequacy of the current stipend. Today, I want to walk you through why this matters for our work—and our reputation."

She advanced to the next slide, a graph showing a sharp decline in on-campus lab usage. "Here’s the reality: since the policy was introduced, our medical annex labs have seen a 40% drop in in-person activity. That’s not because people aren’t working. It’s because they’re working from home. And if they’re working from home, they need the tools to do it effectively."

A hand shot up. Vikram Salian, from the registrar’s office, spoke up. "But Meera, the stipend’s supposed to be a flat rate. If we start making exceptions for research faculty, where does it end? The history department’s going to want book allowances next."

Meera didn’t flinch. "It doesn’t have to be exceptions. It can be a framework. Slide three: *Tiered Stipend Model*." The slide displayed three columns—main campus, medical annex, and liberal-arts satellite—each with a different stipend amount and a list of eligible expenses. "This isn’t about favoring one department over another. It’s about recognizing that different types of work have different needs."

"And the cost?" Vikram pressed. "Where’s the money coming from?"

Meera flipped to the next slide, a pie chart breaking down the university’s discretionary funds. "We’ve identified $250,000 in unallocated funds from last fiscal year. That’s enough to cover the increased stipends for the medical annex and satellite campus faculty for the next two years. After that, we’ll need to reassess—but by then, we’ll have data to show whether this improves retention and productivity."

There was a murmur of agreement around the room. Meera allowed herself a small smile. "And finally, slide six: *Next Steps*. We propose a pilot program starting next semester. IT will handle the tech support side, Procurement will negotiate the vendor discounts, and the research office will track outcomes. Questions?"

Vikram leaned back, arms crossed. "I still think it’s a slippery slope. But... I’ll reserve judgment until I see the pilot results."

"Hey Caio," Gordon started, leaning back in his chair, the glow of his monitor lighting up his face. "We’ve got a problem with the remote work stipend policy rollout. The faculty in the medical annex are pushing back—hard. They say the $500 annual stipend for home office setups isn’t enough, especially for folks running high-end research from their basements."

Caio tapped his fingers on the desk, his browser open to a spreadsheet of budget allocations. "I hear them, but we’re already stretching the [DEPARTMENT_2] budget thin. The main campus faculty got the same offer, and no one’s complained yet. What makes the medical annex special?"

"Special?" Gordon chuckled. "Try running a microbiology lab from your living room. They’re arguing they need stipends for high-speed internet upgrades, not just ergonomic chairs. And Larissa in [DEPARTMENT_3] just sent me an estimate—those upgrades alone could blow past $1,000 per person."

Caio sighed, rubbing his temples. "Okay, but we can’t just hand out blank checks. What if we tier the stipends? Medical annex gets $1,200, main campus stays at $500, and the liberal-arts satellite gets... I dunno, $750? It’s not perfect, but it acknowledges the differences in need."

"Tiered stipends might work," Gordon admitted. "But we’d need to get buy-in from the [DEPARTMENT_1]. And fast. The dean’s been breathing down my neck about retention—if we don’t sort this out, we might lose a couple of our top virologists to places with better remote support."

Caio nodded. "I’ll draft a proposal. You set up a meeting with Meera in the [DEPARTMENT_1]. And Gordon?"

"Yeah?"

"Make sure she knows this isn’t just [DEPARTMENT_2]’s problem. It’s a university-wide retention issue."

Gordon grinned. "You’re the one who’s good at making people feel like they’re part of the solution. Work your magic."
textB:
- "Slide one:
- *Remote Work Stipend Policy – Research Office Perspectives*," [PERSON_3] announced, clicking through her presentation.
- The room was packed with department heads, their attention fixed on the projector screen.
- "As some of you know, the [DEPARTMENT_1] has been fielding concerns from faculty about the adequacy of the current stipend.
- Today, I want to walk you through why this matters for our work—and our reputation."
- She advanced to the next slide, a graph showing a sharp decline in on-campus lab usage.
- "Here’s the reality:
- since the policy was introduced, our medical annex labs have seen a 40% drop in in-person activity.
- That’s not because people aren’t working.
- It’s because they’re working from home.
- And if they’re working from home, they need the tools to do it effectively."
- A hand shot up.
- [PERSON_4], from the registrar’s office, spoke up.
- "But Meera, the stipend’s supposed to be a flat rate.
- If we start making exceptions for research faculty, where does it end?
- The history department’s going to want book allowances next."
- Meera didn’t flinch.
- "It doesn’t have to be exceptions.
- It can be a framework.
- Slide three:
- *Tiered Stipend Model*." The slide displayed three columns—main campus, medical annex, and liberal-arts satellite—each with a different stipend amount and a list of eligible expenses.
- "This isn’t about favoring one department over another.
- It’s about recognizing that different types of work have different needs."
- "And the cost?" Vikram pressed.
- "Where’s the money coming from?"
- Meera flipped to the next slide, a pie chart breaking down the university’s discretionary funds.
- "We’ve identified $250,000 in unallocated funds from last fiscal year.
- That’s enough to cover the increased stipends for the medical annex and satellite campus faculty for the next two years.
- After that, we’ll need to reassess—but by then, we’ll have data to show whether this improves retention and productivity."
- There was a murmur of agreement around the room.
- Meera allowed herself a small smile.
- "And finally, slide six:
- *Next Steps*.
- We propose a pilot program starting next semester.
- [DEPARTMENT_2] will handle the tech support side, [DEPARTMENT_3] will negotiate the vendor discounts, and the [DEPARTMENT_1] will track outcomes.
- Questions?"
- Vikram leaned back, arms crossed.
- "I still think it’s a slippery slope.
- But...
- I’ll reserve judgment until I see the pilot results."

"As some of you know, the research office has been fielding concerns from faculty about the adequacy of the current stipend. Today, I want to walk you through why this matters for our work—and our reputation."

She advanced to the next slide, a graph showing a sharp decline in on-campus lab usage. "Here’s the reality: since the policy was introduced, our medical annex labs have seen a 40% drop in in-person activity. That’s not because people aren’t working. It’s because they’re working from home. And if they’re working from home, they need the tools to do it effectively."

A hand shot up. Vikram Salian, from the registrar’s office, spoke up. "But Meera, the stipend’s supposed to be a flat rate. If we start making exceptions for research faculty, where does it end? The history department’s going to want book allowances next."

Meera didn’t flinch. "It doesn’t have to be exceptions. It can be a framework. Slide three: *Tiered Stipend Model*." The slide displayed three columns—main campus, medical annex, and liberal-arts satellite—each with a different stipend amount and a list of eligible expenses. "This isn’t about favoring one department over another. It’s about recognizing that different types of work have different needs."

"And the cost?" Vikram pressed. "Where’s the money coming from?"

Meera flipped to the next slide, a pie chart breaking down the university’s discretionary funds. "We’ve identified $250,000 in unallocated funds from last fiscal year. That’s enough to cover the increased stipends for the medical annex and satellite campus faculty for the next two years. After that, we’ll need to reassess—but by then, we’ll have data to show whether this improves retention and productivity."

There was a murmur of agreement around the room. Meera allowed herself a small smile. "And finally, slide six: *Next Steps*. We propose a pilot program starting next semester. IT will handle the tech support side, Procurement will negotiate the vendor discounts, and the research office will track outcomes. Questions?"

Vikram leaned back, arms crossed. "I still think it’s a slippery slope. But... I’ll reserve judgment until I see the pilot results."

"Slide 1: Q3 Facilities Budget Overview. Dale, you’re up first," Marlys said, gesturing to the projector screen where a bar chart displayed the campus-wide expenditures. "The board wants to see the breakdown between the main campus, the med school annex, and the liberal-arts satellite. No fluff—just numbers and justifications."

Dale cleared his throat and stepped forward. "Thanks, Marlys. As you can see, the main campus is on track, but the med school annex is over by 8% due to the dining hall upgrades. Sutro Campus Dining Group submitted a change order mid-quarter for the new ventilation system, and we had to approve it to meet health codes."

"And the liberal-arts campus?" Marlys prompted, flipping to the next slide, which showed a pie chart of expenses.

"That’s where it gets tricky," Dale admitted. "We budgeted for routine maintenance, but the old HVAC system in the arts building failed in August. Replacement parts were backordered, so we had to lease temporary units from Oakhurst. That’s the 5% variance you’re seeing here."

Marlys crossed her arms. "So we’re telling the board that unplanned repairs and a vendor’s change order are why we’re over budget? They’re not going to like that."

"We don’t have a choice," Dale said. "But I did pull the invoices and the contracts. We can show them the cost comparisons and the justification memos. It’s not ideal, but it’s transparent."

Marlys sighed. "Alright, we’ll lead with the med school annex—highlight the health code compliance. Then we’ll address the liberal-arts campus as a ‘one-time capital improvement.’ But we need to tie it back to student retention. The board eats that up." Dale nodded, already making notes on his tablet.

"Slide one: *API Gateway Migration – Facilities Impact*," Bev announced, clicking through the presentation. "As you can see, the new gateway sits behind our load balancers, which means we’re responsible for the SSL termination and traffic routing. The problem? The current hardware can’t handle the increased TLS handshake load."

Rohan crossed his arms. "So what’s the ask? New load balancers? Because procurement’s going to want a cost justification, and ‘IT said so’ isn’t going to cut it."

"Exactly," Bev said, advancing to the next slide. "We’ve got two options: upgrade the existing balancers or spin up a cloud-based solution. The latter’s faster but pricier long-term. IT’s leaning toward the cloud route, but facilities would own the maintenance either way."

"And the timeline?" Rohan asked.

"If we go cloud, we’re looking at a week for provisioning. Hardware? Four to six weeks, easy. But here’s the kicker—" Bev paused for effect, "—the satellite campus is still on our old balancers. If we don’t upgrade those too, their systems will choke when the gateway flips over."

Rohan groaned. "So we’re talking about a phased rollout. Facilities upgrades the main campus first, then the annex, then the satellite. But who’s coordinating with the satellite’s facilities team? Because last I heard, they report to a different budget."

"That’s Marlys’s problem," Bev said, grinning. "She’s already in the loop. But we need to lock this down by Friday or IT’s going to start the migration without us."

We need a more robust system, maybe cloud-based, to ensure we’re not losing critical information."

Half the staff still have generic logins, and we’ve got no audit trail for who’s making changes to the inventory. That’s a security risk, especially with the medical school’s sensitive equipment stored there."

"What about the CCTV cameras?" Maya asked. "The ones in the loading dock area are grainy, and half of them don’t even work. If there’s an incident, we won’t have any usable footage."

Raj nodded. "I’ll add that to the list. We’ll need to coordinate with Facilities to get the cameras replaced and the new scanners installed. But first, let’s prioritize the data backup and access controls. Those are quick wins that can be done internally."

*Prepared by: Tatiana Nogueira | Date: [REDACTED] | Version: 0.3*

--- 

**OVERVIEW**
Alright, folks, here’s the *fun* part: where we try to make the numbers work without anyone crying (too much). This year’s research budget is… well, let’s call it *ambitious*. We’ve got a 5% increase from last year, but with inflation and the new grant-matching requirements, it’s gonna feel like we’re trying to squeeze blood from a stone. **BIG EXPENSES**
1. **Lab Equipment Upgrades**: Halden Lab Equipment Co. gave us a quote for $220K to replace the aging centrifuges in the med annex. Ouch. But if we don’t, we’re risking another failed accreditation inspection—and nobody wants *that* email from the dean.

2. **Grant Administration Software**: We’re still using spreadsheets to track grants. *Spreadsheets*. In 2024. I’ve got a demo scheduled with a vendor next week, but their system runs $50K upfront plus $10K/year. Worth it? Probably. Sexy? Not even a little.

3. **Student Research Stipends**: We’ve got 12 more undergrads in the summer program this year, so that’s an extra $36K in stipends. On the bright side, the provost’s office chipped in $15K, so we’re only on the hook for $21K. Small mercies.

**POTENTIAL SAVINGS**
- **Shared Resources**: The biology and chem departments are *finally* agreeing to share a high-end microscope. That saves us $40K we’d’ve spent on a duplicate.
- **Travel Cuts**: We’re trimming conference travel by 10%. Yeah, people will grumble, but unless someone invents teleportation, this is the easiest place to cut.
- **Energy Rebates**: If we time the lab equipment purchases right, we can snag a state energy rebate. That’s $12K back in our pocket if we jump through the right hoops.

**NOTES**
- Still waiting on final numbers from Oakhurst Textbook Wholesale for bulk orders. They promised us a discount if we commit by March.
- Dale in Procurement says he can get us a better deal on office supplies if we bundle with Facilities. I’ll follow up.
- *P.S. If anyone sees Marlys, tell her I still need her signature on the carryover funds form. She’s avoiding me. Again.*

Let’s sync up tomorrow at 2 for a quick stand-up. Bring coffee. 

—Gordon

Alright, so we’re in this meeting—me, Dale, and a couple folks from the med school annex—and we’re trying to figure out how the remote stipend policy plays with research grants. Dale’s kicking it off: 

*Dale*: So, the stipend’s great for admin staff, but what about grad students or postdocs working on grants? Their funding’s already earmarked for specific stuff. If we start letting them tap into this stipend, do we have to rework the grant budgets? 

*Meera*: Ugh, don’t even get me started. Some of these grants have *zero* flexibility. If we’re not careful, we’re basically asking PIs to choose between paying for a student’s home office setup or, y’know, *actual research*. 

*Tati*: But hold on—what if we treat it like a fringe benefit? Some grants already cover things like health insurance. Maybe we can shoehorn this in there? 

*Dale*: Maybe, but we’d have to get sign-off from every single grant agency. And you know how *that* goes. Last time we tried to reclassify something, it took six months and three rounds of emails just to get a ‘maybe.’ 

*Meera*: So what’s the alternative? Tell folks they’re out of luck if they’re on a grant? That’s gonna go over like a lead balloon. 

*Tati*: Well, what if we limit it to non-grant-funded staff for now? At least until we sort out the logistics. Worst case, we pilot it with one department and see how it shakes out. 

*Dale*: Yeah, but then we’re back to square one with equity. If we do this for IT but not for Research, people are gonna cry foul. 

…And that’s about where we left it. No decisions, just a lot of head-scratching. Classic.

SLIDE DECK: API Gateway Migration – Research Office Impact

--- Slide 1: Title ---
‘API Gateway Migration: Why Research Cares (And You Should Too)’
*Presented by: Meera Iyengar & Larissa Camargo*

- Current setup: 12 legacy APIs, all talking to each other like it’s 2010. Slow. Clunky. Embarrassing.

If we don’t address those, we’re looking at compliance fines that’ll dwarf the cost of the upgrades." He turned to the whiteboard, where a rough breakdown of expenses was scribbled in red marker. "What’s the damage if we go with Trellis and still allocate for the security patches?"

Priya pulled up a spreadsheet on her laptop. "If we take Trellis’s offer and trim 10% from the software licensing renewal—maybe negotiate with the vendors for a multi-year deal—we can cover both. But that means delaying the classroom AV upgrades until next fiscal year." She hesitated. "The liberal-arts campus has been pushing for those projections systems for a while now."

"They’ll have to wait," Gordon said firmly. "Security first. Then infrastructure. The AV can be a phase-two project." He scribbled a note to revisit the classroom tech in Q3. "Priya, draft an email to Trellis confirming the terms, and cc Bev in Procurement. She’ll need to fast-track the PO." Priya nodded, already typing. "And Gordon?" she added, looking up. "We should loop in Caio from Facilities. The server room’s cooling system is on its last legs, and if we’re upgrading hardware, we need to ensure the infrastructure can handle it." Gordon groaned. "Right. Add that to the follow-up list. This budget’s turning into a Jenga tower."

"Slide one: *Remote Work Stipend Policy – Research Office Perspectives*," Meera Iyengar announced, clicking through her presentation. The room was packed with department heads, their attention fixed on the projector screen. "As some of you know, the research office has been fielding concerns from faculty about the adequacy of the current stipend. Today, I want to walk you through why this matters for our work—and our reputation."

She advanced to the next slide, a graph showing a sharp decline in on-campus lab usage. "Here’s the reality: since the policy was introduced, our medical annex labs have seen a 40% drop in in-person activity. That’s not because people aren’t working. It’s because they’re working from home. And if they’re working from home, they need the tools to do it effectively."

A hand shot up. Vikram Salian, from the registrar’s office, spoke up. "But Meera, the stipend’s supposed to be a flat rate. If we start making exceptions for research faculty, where does it end? The history department’s going to want book allowances next."

Meera didn’t flinch. "It doesn’t have to be exceptions. It can be a framework. Slide three: *Tiered Stipend Model*." The slide displayed three columns—main campus, medical annex, and liberal-arts satellite—each with a different stipend amount and a list of eligible expenses. "This isn’t about favoring one department over another. It’s about recognizing that different types of work have different needs."

"And the cost?" Vikram pressed. "Where’s the money coming from?"

Meera flipped to the next slide, a pie chart breaking down the university’s discretionary funds. "We’ve identified $250,000 in unallocated funds from last fiscal year. That’s enough to cover the increased stipends for the medical annex and satellite campus faculty for the next two years. After that, we’ll need to reassess—but by then, we’ll have data to show whether this improves retention and productivity."

There was a murmur of agreement around the room. Meera allowed herself a small smile. "And finally, slide six: *Next Steps*. We propose a pilot program starting next semester. IT will handle the tech support side, Procurement will negotiate the vendor discounts, and the research office will track outcomes. Questions?"

Vikram leaned back, arms crossed. "I still think it’s a slippery slope. But... I’ll reserve judgment until I see the pilot results."

Sutro’s been supplying office snacks and coffee for faculty lounges, but with more people working remotely, their on-campus sales have dropped 30%. They’re asking if we can redirect some of the stipend budget to bulk deliveries of coffee and snacks to faculty homes."

Dale Rambow, who’d been quietly taking notes, spoke up. "What about the equipment vendors? Trellis Research Computing reached out last week. They’re offering a 15% discount on high-performance laptops if we commit to a bulk order for remote faculty. Could we fold that into the stipend policy as an optional add-on?"

Larissa leaned forward. "That’s... actually not a bad idea. If we can negotiate a university-wide discount, faculty could use part of their stipend to upgrade their hardware through an approved vendor. It keeps the money in our ecosystem and gives folks more flexibility."

"But what about equity?" Bev asked. "Not everyone needs a high-end laptop. The liberal-arts faculty might prefer to spend their stipend on books or a second monitor."

Larissa nodded. "Then we make it optional. The stipend stays cash, but we provide a list of pre-approved vendors and discounts for those who want to use it that way. And we document everything so Finance doesn’t come knocking."

"Today’s agenda: the remote work stipend policy’s impact on our vendor contracts. Bev, you’re up first—how’s Sutro Campus Dining Group handling the shift?"

Sutro’s been supplying office snacks and coffee for faculty lounges, but with more people working remotely, their on-campus sales have dropped 30%. They’re asking if we can redirect some of the stipend budget to bulk deliveries of coffee and snacks to faculty homes."

Larissa raised an eyebrow. "So they want us to turn stipends into a meal-per-diem situation? That’s not what this policy was designed for."

"I know, I know," Bev said, holding up her hands. "But they’re a long-term partner, and they’re hurting. If we don’t work with them, they might pull out of the medical annex entirely. And then who’s going to keep the med students caffeinated during all-nighters?"

Dale Rambow, who’d been quietly taking notes, spoke up. "What about the equipment vendors? Trellis Research Computing reached out last week. They’re offering a 15% discount on high-performance laptops if we commit to a bulk order for remote faculty. Could we fold that into the stipend policy as an optional add-on?"

Larissa leaned forward. "That’s... actually not a bad idea. If we can negotiate a university-wide discount, faculty could use part of their stipend to upgrade their hardware through an approved vendor. It keeps the money in our ecosystem and gives folks more flexibility."

"But what about equity?" Bev asked. "Not everyone needs a high-end laptop. The liberal-arts faculty might prefer to spend their stipend on books or a second monitor."

Larissa nodded. "Then we make it optional. The stipend stays cash, but we provide a list of pre-approved vendors and discounts for those who want to use it that way. And we document everything so Finance doesn’t come knocking."

"We don’t have a choice," Dale said. "But I did pull the invoices and the contracts. We can show them the cost comparisons and the justification memos. It’s not ideal, but it’s transparent."

Marlys sighed. "Alright, we’ll lead with the med school annex—highlight the health code compliance. Then we’ll address the liberal-arts campus as a ‘one-time capital improvement.’ But we need to tie it back to student retention. The board eats that up." Dale nodded, already making notes on his tablet.

Alright, folks, here’s the *fun* part: where we try to make the numbers work without anyone crying (too much). This year’s research budget is… well, let’s call it *ambitious*. Ananya added, "Also, reach out to the IT department. They’ve been sitting on some unallocated cloud computing credits. If we can trade those for lab equipment, we might free up cash."

"Good call," Rohan said, jotting notes. "I’ll have a revised budget to you by end of day. But Ananya, we need to present this to the deans next week. They won’t like the cuts."

"Slide one: *API Gateway Migration – Facilities Impact*," Bev announced, clicking through the presentation. "As you can see, the new gateway sits behind our load balancers, which means we’re responsible for the SSL termination and traffic routing. The problem? The current hardware can’t handle the increased TLS handshake load."

Rohan crossed his arms. "So what’s the ask? New load balancers? Because procurement’s going to want a cost justification, and ‘IT said so’ isn’t going to cut it."

"Exactly," Bev said, advancing to the next slide. "We’ve got two options: upgrade the existing balancers or spin up a cloud-based solution. The latter’s faster but pricier long-term. IT’s leaning toward the cloud route, but facilities would own the maintenance either way."

"And the timeline?" Rohan asked.

"If we go cloud, we’re looking at a week for provisioning. Hardware? Four to six weeks, easy. But here’s the kicker—" Bev paused for effect, "—the satellite campus is still on our old balancers. If we don’t upgrade those too, their systems will choke when the gateway flips over."

Rohan groaned. "So we’re talking about a phased rollout. Facilities upgrades the main campus first, then the annex, then the satellite. But who’s coordinating with the satellite’s facilities team? Because last I heard, they report to a different budget."

"That’s Marlys’s problem," Bev said, grinning. "She’s already in the loop. But we need to lock this down by Friday or IT’s going to start the migration without us."

The room was packed with department heads, all clutching printed agendas. "Our biggest challenge? Balancing the medical school’s grant-funded projects with the liberal-arts campus’s push for interdisciplinary research initiatives."

Slide 3: Budget Breakdown
- Grant Allocations: $2.4M (60% to medical school, 30% to main campus, 10% to satellite)
- Equipment & Supplies: $850K (new microscopes for medical annex, shared lab spaces)
- Personnel: $1.2M (hiring two postdocs, part-time research assistants)

"Here’s where it gets tricky," Larissa said, pointing to the personnel line. "We’ve got approval for the postdocs, but the dean wants us to absorb the cost of a new IRB coordinator. That’s an additional $90K we hadn’t planned for."

Slide 4: Proposed Adjustments
- Reallocate 5% from equipment to personnel (delay microscope purchase by one quarter)
- Seek cost-sharing with IT for data storage upgrades (estimated $50K savings)
- Negotiate bulk discounts with Oakhurst Textbook Wholesale for research materials

"Vikram, you’re shaking your head," Larissa noted, pausing as Vikram Salian, the research grants manager, spoke up. "The microscopes are tied to a time-sensitive NIH grant. If we delay, we risk losing the funding entirely." Larissa sighed. "Then we’ll have to find another $90K. Maybe we tap into the contingency fund, but that’ll mean cutting the student research stipends by 20%."

Slide 5: Next Steps
- Finalize adjustments by November 15
- Submit to provost’s office for approval
- Communicate changes to department chairs by December 1

"This isn’t pretty," Larissa admitted, "but it’s the best we can do without derailing critical projects. Any objections?" The room fell silent. Vikram exchanged a glance with Meera Iyengar from the registrar’s office. "I’ll need to see the revised stipend numbers," Meera said finally. *Prepared by: Tatiana Nogueira | Date: [REDACTED] | Version: 0.3*

**OVERVIEW**
Alright, folks, here’s the *fun* part: where we try to make the numbers work without anyone crying (too much). This year’s research budget is… well, let’s call it *ambitious*. We’ve got a 5% increase from last year, but with inflation and the new grant-matching requirements, it’s gonna feel like we’re trying to squeeze blood from a stone. - **Travel Cuts**: We’re trimming conference travel by 10%. Yeah, people will grumble, but unless someone invents teleportation, this is the easiest place to cut.
- **Energy Rebates**: If we time the lab equipment purchases right, we can snag a state energy rebate. That’s $12K back in our pocket if we jump through the right hoops.

"Okay, let’s start with the pain points," Meera said, tapping her pen against the table. "Last semester, we had 47 freshmen drop out before week three because they couldn’t navigate the portal. That’s not just a tech issue—it’s a trust issue."

"I hear that," Larissa replied, leaning forward. "But the current onboarding emails are a mess. Three different departments send welcome packets, and half the links are dead by October. We need a single source of truth."

"Exactly," Meera nodded. "And the portal’s UI looks like it was designed in 2005. Caio’s team could help, but IT’s backlog is a mile long. Maybe we pilot a simplified dashboard for the liberal-arts campus first? Smaller user base, easier to test."

Larissa scribbled on her notepad. "What if we tie it to the registrar’s new ID card system? One login, one profile. Students hate carrying three different cards."

"That’s smart," Meera said. "But we’d need buy-in from Dale. He’s protective of the registrar’s data. Still, if we frame it as reducing duplicate work—"

"—he’ll listen," Larissa finished. "I’ll set up a meeting with him and the IT liaison. You draft the student feedback survey. We’ll need hard numbers to sell this to the provost."

"Deal," Meera said. "But let’s not forget the medical school annex. Their onboarding’s even worse—different compliance forms, different deadlines. If we can crack that, the main campus will follow."

Okay, so this is a scanned PDF of the *very* official-looking draft of the remote work stipend policy that Bev’s been circulating. It’s got all the legalese and fine print you’d expect, but I’ll spare you the jargon and give you the gist. 

First off, the stipend’s only for employees classified as ‘regular, non-temporary’—so no grad students, adjuncts, or temp workers. Bummer, I know. It’s also prorated if you’re only remote part-time, which, honestly, feels like a way to nickel-and-dime folks, but hey, I don’t make the rules. 

The big debate right now is whether to handle this as a taxable benefit or just straight-up payroll. Bev’s leaning toward taxable because, quote, ‘the IRS is not our friend in this scenario.’ If we go that route, employees would see the stipend on their W-2s, which means they’d owe taxes on it. Not ideal, but apparently the alternative is even messier. 

There’s also a whole section on ‘eligible expenses,’ which includes things like internet, office furniture, and even software subscriptions (as long as they’re work-related). But here’s the catch: you’ve got to submit receipts, and anything over $100 needs pre-approval. So if you’re eyeing that $1,200 Herman Miller chair, you’re out of luck unless you get sign-off first. 

Oh, and get this—there’s a clause about ‘clawbacks.’ If you leave the university within a year of getting the stipend, you might have to pay it back. Because, of course, we can’t just make things *easy*. 

Anyway, Bev’s got a redline version with about a hundred comments from Legal, so who knows what the final version’ll look like. Fingers crossed it doesn’t get watered down into oblivion.

"So, Bev, the HVAC system in the liberal-arts campus is on its last legs," Dale Rambow said, flipping through a thick binder of inspection reports. "The estimate from the vendor is $220K, but if we wait another year, we’re looking at emergency repairs that could double that cost."

Bev Koepper crossed her arms. "And the main campus roof? The leaks in the science building are getting worse. Students are complaining about damaged equipment in the research labs. That’s a liability issue."

"Right," Dale admitted. "The roof is $180K, but we’ve got a grant application pending with the research office for partial funding. If that comes through, we could split the difference. But the HVAC is time-sensitive."

"What about the medical annex?" Bev asked. "I heard they’re pushing for a new chiller system."

Dale groaned. "They are, and it’s another $150K. But here’s the thing—their current system is under warranty until June. If we can stretch it to July, we might align the replacement with the next fiscal year’s budget."

Bev tapped her fingers on the table. "Okay, let’s rank these. HVAC first, then the roof, then the chiller. But we need to get the research office’s grant status in writing. And Dale, see if we can get a bulk discount from the HVAC vendor if we bundle the liberal-arts campus and the annex."

"I’ll reach out to Trellis Research Computing too," Dale added. "They’ve been talking about energy-efficient servers. Maybe we can piggyback on their upgrades for some cost savings."

Bev smiled. "Good. But let’s get this in a report by Friday. I need to present it to the provost next week."

Slide 1: Remote Work Stipend Policy – What Researchers Need to Know

Hey, team! If you’re reading this, odds are you’re either (a) working from home in your pajamas or (b) *wishing* you were. Either way, here’s the deal on the stipend.

Slide 2: The Basics
- $1,200 max per employee every 2 years. Yes, that includes you, even if you’re based at the liberal-arts campus.
- Covers: desks, chairs, monitors, laptops (if your current one’s older than a dinosaur), and *some* software. Check the full list on the intranet.

- Receipts *must* be uploaded to the research office’s portal within 30 days. No receipt? No stipend. No exceptions.
- Manager approval is *mandatory*. If your PI doesn’t sign off, you’re SOL.
- Hybrid workers: you’re eligible, but you can’t double-dip if you’ve already used the stipend for on-campus gear.

- If you’re ordering lab equipment (looking at you, biology folks), that’s a *separate* budget. This stipend’s for *your* workspace, not your petri dishes.

Q: Can I use this for a second monitor?
A: Yes, but if you already have three, maybe reconsider your life choices.

Q: What if I move mid-stipend?
A: Tough luck. The stipend’s tied to your current role, not your future digs.

A: …No. But we *do* have a ‘pets of the research office’ Slack channel. Just saying.

2. Data repository syncs could stall if IP whitelists aren’t updated.
3. IRB system downtime during cutover.
Speaker Notes: "Vikram, your team handles the grant submissions. What’s your timeline for testing the new auth flow?"

Slide 4: Mitigation Plan
- Phase 1: Test OAuth2 flow with a subset of researchers (Week 1).
- Phase 2: Update IP whitelists and validate data repository syncs (Week 2).
- Phase 3: Full cutover during low-activity window (Week 3).
Speaker Notes: "We’ll need IT’s support to validate the token migration. Gordon, can we get a dedicated window for this?"

Slide 5: Open Questions
- Will the new gateway support our legacy SOAP endpoints?
- Are there costs associated with increased API calls?

Ananya tapped her pen on the desk. "I’ve been hearing the same from advisors. The medical annex students especially struggle with the dual-campus verification step. Maybe we split the process into two tracks: main campus and medical/satellite. Each gets tailored prompts."

"That’s a start," Gordon said, "but we’d need IT to tweak the backend. And Facilities might have to adjust the physical welcome packets—if we’re changing the digital side, the paper handouts should match. Can you loop in Caio from IT and Bev from Facilities? I’ll draft the high-level requirements by EOD."

Ananya nodded. "I’ll set up a working group meeting for Thursday. We’ll need data on where exactly they’re stalling—maybe heatmaps of the upload page. And let’s check if the registrar’s office has any pre-existing forms we can repurpose instead of building from scratch."

"Good call," Gordon replied. "Also, let’s not forget the liberal-arts campus—they’ve got their own quirks with transfer credits. We’ll need to test the new flow with a small cohort there first. I’ll ask Larissa to coordinate that pilot."

textB:
"Slide one: *Remote Work Stipend Policy – Research Office Perspectives*," Meera Iyengar announced, clicking through her presentation. The room was packed with department heads, their attention fixed on the projector screen. "As some of you know, the research office has been fielding concerns from faculty about the adequacy of the current stipend. Today, I want to walk you through why this matters for our work—and our reputation."

She advanced to the next slide, a graph showing a sharp decline in on-campus lab usage. "Here’s the reality: since the policy was introduced, our medical annex labs have seen a 40% drop in in-person activity. That’s not because people aren’t working. It’s because they’re working from home. And if they’re working from home, they need the tools to do it effectively."

A hand shot up. Vikram Salian, from the registrar’s office, spoke up. "But Meera, the stipend’s supposed to be a flat rate. If we start making exceptions for research faculty, where does it end? The history department’s going to want book allowances next."

Meera didn’t flinch. "It doesn’t have to be exceptions. It can be a framework. Slide three: *Tiered Stipend Model*." The slide displayed three columns—main campus, medical annex, and liberal-arts satellite—each with a different stipend amount and a list of eligible expenses. "This isn’t about favoring one department over another. It’s about recognizing that different types of work have different needs."

"And the cost?" Vikram pressed. "Where’s the money coming from?"

Meera flipped to the next slide, a pie chart breaking down the university’s discretionary funds. "We’ve identified $250,000 in unallocated funds from last fiscal year. That’s enough to cover the increased stipends for the medical annex and satellite campus faculty for the next two years. After that, we’ll need to reassess—but by then, we’ll have data to show whether this improves retention and productivity."

There was a murmur of agreement around the room. Meera allowed herself a small smile. "And finally, slide six: *Next Steps*. We propose a pilot program starting next semester. IT will handle the tech support side, Procurement will negotiate the vendor discounts, and the research office will track outcomes. Questions?"

Vikram leaned back, arms crossed. "I still think it’s a slippery slope. But... I’ll reserve judgment until I see the pilot results."

Hey team, so we’re finally kicking off that API gateway migration we’ve been talking about for ages. Yeah, I know, I know—it’s been on the backburner forever, but with the new semester rolling in, we’ve got to get our act together. The old gateway’s been limping along, and honestly, it’s a miracle it hasn’t crapped out on us yet. So here’s the plan: we’re moving everything to the new Kong setup. Why Kong? Well, it’s got the plugins we need, it’s scalable, and—let’s be real—it’s not the clunky mess we’re currently dealing with. 

Ananya’s already spun up a test instance over on the dev cluster (shoutout to her for putting up with my late-night Slack pings). We’ll need to migrate the student-services APIs first since they’re the most critical—enrollment, financial aid, all that fun stuff. Facilities is next on the list because, let’s face it, if the HVAC system API goes down, we’ll have a mutiny on our hands. 

I’ve attached a rough timeline (yes, it’s color-coded, don’t judge me). Aiming to have Phase 1 done by the end of the month. If anyone sees a problem—or, heaven forbid, a better way to do this—speak up now. Last thing we need is to realize halfway through that we missed something obvious. 

Oh, and if anyone from registrar or procurement is lurking on this thread: we’ll need your input on the auth tokens. The new gateway’s pickier about that stuff, so we’ll have to reissue a few. 

Let’s sync up tomorrow at 2 for a quick stand-up. Bring coffee. 

—Gordon

Hey team,

So, we’ve been hearing a lot of feedback from new students about how clunky our onboarding process is—like, *really* clunky. Between the paper forms, the back-and-forth emails, and the fact that half the links in our welcome packet are dead, it’s no wonder folks are pulling their hair out. Ananya and I were chatting over coffee (shoutout to Sutro’s new cold brew, btw), and we think it’s high time we gave this thing a total glow-up.

Here’s the game plan: First, we’re ditching the PDFs. No one reads those anyway. Instead, we’ll move everything to a slick, mobile-friendly portal. Think one-stop shop—registration, housing forms, even that weird waiver for the rock-climbing wall in the rec center. Second, we’re cutting the number of steps in half. Right now, it takes, like, 17 clicks just to upload a transcript. That’s *ridiculous*. And third, we’re adding a chatbot (yes, I know, I know, but hear me out) to answer FAQs so students aren’t stuck waiting three days for a response about their meal plan.

We’ll need IT to greenlight the portal backend, and facilities to confirm the rec center waiver can live digitally. Also, if anyone’s got a line on a vendor who does *good* chatbots (not the kind that just says ‘I’ll connect you to a human’), hit me up. Let’s get this rolling before the fall rush.

Cheers,
Gordon

P.S. If you see Marlys, tell her I still owe her a coffee for the last time she bailed me out of a spreadsheet disaster.

Slide 1: Annual Budget Planning – Research Office
Subtitle: Fiscal Year 2025 Projections | Presented by Dr. Larissa Camargo

Slide 2: "Good afternoon, everyone. Today, we’re walking through the research office’s budget priorities for the coming year," Larissa Camargo began, clicking to the next slide. The room was packed with department heads, all clutching printed agendas. "Our biggest challenge? Balancing the medical school’s grant-funded projects with the liberal-arts campus’s push for interdisciplinary research initiatives."

Slide 3: Budget Breakdown
- Grant Allocations: $2.4M (60% to medical school, 30% to main campus, 10% to satellite)
- Equipment & Supplies: $850K (new microscopes for medical annex, shared lab spaces)
- Personnel: $1.2M (hiring two postdocs, part-time research assistants)

"Here’s where it gets tricky," Larissa said, pointing to the personnel line. "We’ve got approval for the postdocs, but the dean wants us to absorb the cost of a new IRB coordinator. That’s an additional $90K we hadn’t planned for."

Slide 4: Proposed Adjustments
- Reallocate 5% from equipment to personnel (delay microscope purchase by one quarter)
- Seek cost-sharing with IT for data storage upgrades (estimated $50K savings)
- Negotiate bulk discounts with Oakhurst Textbook Wholesale for research materials

"Vikram, you’re shaking your head," Larissa noted, pausing as Vikram Salian, the research grants manager, spoke up. "The microscopes are tied to a time-sensitive NIH grant. If we delay, we risk losing the funding entirely." Larissa sighed. "Then we’ll have to find another $90K. Maybe we tap into the contingency fund, but that’ll mean cutting the student research stipends by 20%."

Slide 5: Next Steps
- Finalize adjustments by November 15
- Submit to provost’s office for approval
- Communicate changes to department chairs by December 1

"This isn’t pretty," Larissa admitted, "but it’s the best we can do without derailing critical projects. Any objections?" The room fell silent. Vikram exchanged a glance with Meera Iyengar from the registrar’s office. "I’ll need to see the revised stipend numbers," Meera said finally. "If we’re cutting student funding, we’ll have to adjust the financial aid projections accordingly." Larissa nodded. "Send me your figures, and I’ll fold them in."

SLIDE DECK: API Gateway Migration – Research Office Impact

--- Slide 1: Title ---
‘API Gateway Migration: Why Research Cares (And You Should Too)’
*Presented by: Meera Iyengar & Larissa Camargo*

--- Slide 2: The Problem ---
- Current setup: 12 legacy APIs, all talking to each other like it’s 2010. Slow. Clunky. Embarrassing.
- New gateway: Faster, scalier, and—here’s the kicker—*auditable*. (Yes, finally. The feds will weep with joy.)
- Catch: Some of our grant-tracking endpoints are *very* attached to the old system. Like, ‘refuses to leave the nest’ attached.

--- Slide 3: What’s Changing ---
- /grants/submit → Migrating Week 1 (Larissa’s team owns this one. Pray for her.)
- /compliance/reports → Week 2 (Meera’s ‘fun’ project). 
- /collab/partners → Week 3 (If we’re lucky. If not, Week ‘Whenever IT Stops Panicking’).
- Everything else: ‘We’ll cross that bridge when we burn it.’

--- Slide 4: Risks (aka ‘Reasons to Drink’) ---
- Data loss: Unlikely, but if it happens, we’re blaming the medical school’s ‘unique’ firewall rules.
- Downtime: 30 mins max per endpoint. (Ha. We all know it’ll be 2 hours.)
- User confusion: High. Faculty will *definitely* call the helpdesk to ask why their ‘perfectly good’ 2015 bookmark doesn’t work.

--- Slide 5: Action Items ---
- Research PIs: Test your integrations *before* we flip the switch. No, we won’t ‘just delay it.’
- IT: For the love of all things holy, *document the new auth tokens*. 
- Everyone: If you see Caio, buy him a coffee. He’s earned it.

--- Slide 6: Q&A ---
(Prepare for chaos.)

Oh, and if anyone from registrar or procurement is lurking on this thread: we’ll need your input on the auth tokens. The new gateway’s pickier about that stuff, so we’ll have to reissue a few.

—Gordon

"Slide one: *Remote Work Stipend Policy – Research Office Perspectives*," Meera Iyengar announced, clicking through her presentation. The room was packed with department heads, their attention fixed on the projector screen. "As some of you know, the research office has been fielding concerns from faculty about the adequacy of the current stipend. Today, I want to walk you through why this matters for our work—and our reputation."

She advanced to the next slide, a graph showing a sharp decline in on-campus lab usage. "Here’s the reality: since the policy was introduced, our medical annex labs have seen a 40% drop in in-person activity. That’s not because people aren’t working. It’s because they’re working from home. And if they’re working from home, they need the tools to do it effectively."

A hand shot up. Vikram Salian, from the registrar’s office, spoke up. "But Meera, the stipend’s supposed to be a flat rate. If we start making exceptions for research faculty, where does it end? The history department’s going to want book allowances next."

Meera didn’t flinch. "It doesn’t have to be exceptions. It can be a framework. Slide three: *Tiered Stipend Model*." The slide displayed three columns—main campus, medical annex, and liberal-arts satellite—each with a different stipend amount and a list of eligible expenses. "This isn’t about favoring one department over another. It’s about recognizing that different types of work have different needs."

"And the cost?" Vikram pressed. "Where’s the money coming from?"

Meera flipped to the next slide, a pie chart breaking down the university’s discretionary funds. "We’ve identified $250,000 in unallocated funds from last fiscal year. That’s enough to cover the increased stipends for the medical annex and satellite campus faculty for the next two years. After that, we’ll need to reassess—but by then, we’ll have data to show whether this improves retention and productivity."

There was a murmur of agreement around the room. Meera allowed herself a small smile. "And finally, slide six: *Next Steps*. We propose a pilot program starting next semester. IT will handle the tech support side, Procurement will negotiate the vendor discounts, and the research office will track outcomes. Questions?"

Vikram leaned back, arms crossed. "I still think it’s a slippery slope. But... I’ll reserve judgment until I see the pilot results."

Alright, so we’re in this meeting—me, Dale, and a couple folks from the med school annex—and we’re trying to figure out how the remote stipend policy plays with research grants. Dale’s kicking it off: 

*Dale*: So, the stipend’s great for admin staff, but what about grad students or postdocs working on grants? Their funding’s already earmarked for specific stuff. If we start letting them tap into this stipend, do we have to rework the grant budgets? 

*Meera*: Ugh, don’t even get me started. Some of these grants have *zero* flexibility. If we’re not careful, we’re basically asking PIs to choose between paying for a student’s home office setup or, y’know, *actual research*. 

*Tati*: But hold on—what if we treat it like a fringe benefit? Some grants already cover things like health insurance. Maybe we can shoehorn this in there? 

*Dale*: Maybe, but we’d have to get sign-off from every single grant agency. And you know how *that* goes. Last time we tried to reclassify something, it took six months and three rounds of emails just to get a ‘maybe.’ 

*Meera*: So what’s the alternative? Tell folks they’re out of luck if they’re on a grant? That’s gonna go over like a lead balloon. 

*Tati*: Well, what if we limit it to non-grant-funded staff for now? At least until we sort out the logistics. Worst case, we pilot it with one department and see how it shakes out. 

*Dale*: Yeah, but then we’re back to square one with equity. If we do this for IT but not for Research, people are gonna cry foul. 

…And that’s about where we left it. No decisions, just a lot of head-scratching. Classic.

"Right now, grad students in the research office have to jump through hoops just to access lab spaces. They fill out a paper form, get it stamped by their PI, then wait for Facilities to assign a keycard. It’s 2024—this should be digital."

Rohan, who’d been scribbling notes, looked up. "But the medical annex has stricter compliance rules. If we digitize this, we’ll need to ensure the system can handle HIPAA and IRB clearances. Can’t just port over the main campus workflow."

"Exactly," Meera said, advancing to the next slide. "Slide two: ‘Proposed Solution.’ We create a tiered onboarding module. Tier one is basic access—ID verification, emergency contacts. Tier two is research-specific: lab safety training, PI approval, compliance checks. The system auto-advances them based on their program."

"And Facilities?" Rohan asked. "They’ll still need to issue physical keycards for high-security labs."

"Hybrid model," Meera replied. "Digital approvals trigger the keycard request. Facilities gets a dashboard to batch-print them daily. No more chasing down PIs for signatures." She paused. "Slide three: ‘Stakeholders.’ We’ll need buy-in from IT for the backend, Student Services for the student-facing side, and Facilities for the physical access piece. I’ve already talked to Bev in Facilities—she’s on board if we can guarantee the system integrates with their existing keycard software."

Rohan nodded. "And the timeline?"

"Pilot with the fall cohort in the research office," Meera said. "If it works, we scale to the medical annex by spring. But we’ll need IT to prioritize this—Caio’s team is already swamped with the undergrad portal revamp."

"Alright, let’s get this budget finalized before the provost’s office starts breathing down our necks," said Gordon Altvater, tapping his pen on the conference table. The IT department’s annual budget meeting was in full swing, and the tension was palpable. Across from him, Priya Mehta, the newly hired systems analyst, flipped through a stack of vendor quotes. "Gordon, we’ve got three bids for the server upgrades. Trellis Research Computing is offering a 15% discount if we sign by the end of the month, but Bramwell’s leasing option might free up capital for the cybersecurity overhaul we’ve been putting off."

Gordon leaned back, rubbing his temples. "Cybersecurity can’t wait another year. Last quarter’s audit flagged two critical vulnerabilities in the medical school’s network. If we don’t address those, we’re looking at compliance fines that’ll dwarf the cost of the upgrades." He turned to the whiteboard, where a rough breakdown of expenses was scribbled in red marker. "What’s the damage if we go with Trellis and still allocate for the security patches?"

Priya pulled up a spreadsheet on her laptop. "If we take Trellis’s offer and trim 10% from the software licensing renewal—maybe negotiate with the vendors for a multi-year deal—we can cover both. But that means delaying the classroom AV upgrades until next fiscal year." She hesitated. "The liberal-arts campus has been pushing for those projections systems for a while now."

"They’ll have to wait," Gordon said firmly. "Security first. Then infrastructure. The AV can be a phase-two project." He scribbled a note to revisit the classroom tech in Q3. "Priya, draft an email to Trellis confirming the terms, and cc Bev in Procurement. She’ll need to fast-track the PO." Priya nodded, already typing. "And Gordon?" she added, looking up. "We should loop in Caio from Facilities. The server room’s cooling system is on its last legs, and if we’re upgrading hardware, we need to ensure the infrastructure can handle it." Gordon groaned. "Right. Add that to the follow-up list. This budget’s turning into a Jenga tower."

The IT department’s annual budget meeting was in full swing, and the tension was palpable. Across from him, Priya Mehta, the newly hired systems analyst, flipped through a stack of vendor quotes. "Gordon, we’ve got three bids for the server upgrades. Trellis Research Computing is offering a 15% discount if we sign by the end of the month, but Bramwell’s leasing option might free up capital for the cybersecurity overhaul we’ve been putting off."

A: Yes, but if you already have three, maybe reconsider your life choices.

"So, Bev, the HVAC system in the liberal-arts campus is on its last legs," Dale Rambow said, flipping through a thick binder of inspection reports. "The estimate from the vendor is $220K, but if we wait another year, we’re looking at emergency repairs that could double that cost."

Bev Koepper crossed her arms. "And the main campus roof? The leaks in the science building are getting worse. Students are complaining about damaged equipment in the research labs. That’s a liability issue."

"Right," Dale admitted. "The roof is $180K, but we’ve got a grant application pending with the research office for partial funding. If that comes through, we could split the difference. But the HVAC is time-sensitive."

"What about the medical annex?" Bev asked. "I heard they’re pushing for a new chiller system."

Dale groaned. "They are, and it’s another $150K. But here’s the thing—their current system is under warranty until June. If we can stretch it to July, we might align the replacement with the next fiscal year’s budget."

Bev tapped her fingers on the table. "Okay, let’s rank these. HVAC first, then the roof, then the chiller. But we need to get the research office’s grant status in writing. And Dale, see if we can get a bulk discount from the HVAC vendor if we bundle the liberal-arts campus and the annex."

"I’ll reach out to Trellis Research Computing too," Dale added. "They’ve been talking about energy-efficient servers. Maybe we can piggyback on their upgrades for some cost savings."

Bev smiled. "Good. But let’s get this in a report by Friday. I need to present it to the provost next week."

"Slide one: *API Gateway Migration – Facilities Impact*," Bev announced, clicking through the presentation. "As you can see, the new gateway sits behind our load balancers, which means we’re responsible for the SSL termination and traffic routing. The problem? The current hardware can’t handle the increased TLS handshake load."

Rohan crossed his arms. "So what’s the ask? New load balancers? Because procurement’s going to want a cost justification, and ‘IT said so’ isn’t going to cut it."

"Exactly," Bev said, advancing to the next slide. "We’ve got two options: upgrade the existing balancers or spin up a cloud-based solution. The latter’s faster but pricier long-term. IT’s leaning toward the cloud route, but facilities would own the maintenance either way."

"And the timeline?" Rohan asked.

"If we go cloud, we’re looking at a week for provisioning. Hardware? Four to six weeks, easy. But here’s the kicker—" Bev paused for effect, "—the satellite campus is still on our old balancers. If we don’t upgrade those too, their systems will choke when the gateway flips over."

Rohan groaned. "So we’re talking about a phased rollout. Facilities upgrades the main campus first, then the annex, then the satellite. But who’s coordinating with the satellite’s facilities team? Because last I heard, they report to a different budget."

"That’s Marlys’s problem," Bev said, grinning. "She’s already in the loop. But we need to lock this down by Friday or IT’s going to start the migration without us."

- June: Finalize requirements (and stop changing them, for the love of all things holy).
- July: IT builds the backend. We’ll provide coffee. And maybe donuts.
- August: Beta test with summer students. Pray nothing breaks.
- September: Full rollout. Cross fingers. Light candles. Sacrifice a stapler to the tech gods.

- Admissions: *Please* stop ‘temporarily’ adding new fields.
- IT: We need that API doc *yesterday*.
- Everyone: If you see a student with a paper form, *gently* direct them to the new portal. Or just take it and burn it. Your call.

"Ananya, the grant allocations are finalized, but we’ve got a problem," Rohan Deshpande said, sliding a printed budget sheet across the table. "The NIH cut our expected funding by 12%. That’s $90K we were counting on for the biomedical research labs."

Ananya Krishnan frowned, scanning the document. "And the NSF? Any word on the pending proposals?"

"Still under review," Rohan replied. "But the timeline’s tight. We need to reallocate or find new sources. The medical school annex is pushing for a new MRI machine, but that’s a $500K line item we can’t cover now."

Ananya tapped her pen. "What about the internal research fund? We’ve got $40K unspent from last year’s carryover. Not enough for the MRI, but maybe we can redirect it to the labs hit by the NIH cut."

"That’s a start," Rohan said. "But we’ll need more. The facilities department is asking for co-funding on the HVAC upgrades for the research buildings. If we chip in, they might prioritize our labs."

"Let’s see the numbers," Ananya said. "If we take $20K from the internal fund and another $30K from the discretionary budget, we can cover the NIH shortfall. But the MRI is still a gap. Maybe we can lease instead of buy?"

Rohan nodded. "I’ll talk to Trellis about leasing options. And I’ll check with the procurement office—maybe they can negotiate better terms with Halden for the lab equipment we do need."

Ananya added, "Also, reach out to the IT department. They’ve been sitting on some unallocated cloud computing credits. If we can trade those for lab equipment, we might free up cash."

"Good call," Rohan said, jotting notes. "I’ll have a revised budget to you by end of day. But Ananya, we need to present this to the deans next week. They won’t like the cuts."

"They won’t," Ananya agreed. "But better to be transparent now than surprise them later."

"Alright, team, let’s sync on the API gateway migration," Gordon said, leaning forward in his chair. "We’ve got the medical school annex running on the old system, and the liberal-arts campus is already half-migrated. Ananya crossed her arms. "The auth layer is the sticking point. The old gateway uses a legacy LDAP bind that the new system doesn’t support out of the box. We either refactor the auth middleware or spin up a temporary bridge."

Ananya nodded. "I’ll pull the current rules from the old gateway tomorrow and draft a translation table. If we can get the bridge live by Friday, we can test against the liberal-arts campus first—they’ve got lower traffic."

"Good call," Caio said. "But we need to loop in Marlys from facilities. Their building management APIs are still hitting the old endpoint. If we flip the switch without warning, their HVAC monitoring could go dark."

Gordon sighed. "I’ll ping Marlys after this. Meanwhile, let’s get the bridge deployed and start the auth middleware refactor in parallel. No more delays—this migration’s already three weeks behind schedule."

Slide 1: Remote Work Stipend Policy – What Researchers Need to Know

Hey, team! If you’re reading this, odds are you’re either (a) working from home in your pajamas or (b) *wishing* you were. Either way, here’s the deal on the stipend.

Slide 2: The Basics
- $1,200 max per employee every 2 years. Yes, that includes you, even if you’re based at the liberal-arts campus.
- Covers: desks, chairs, monitors, laptops (if your current one’s older than a dinosaur), and *some* software. Check the full list on the intranet.
- Does *not* cover: snacks, plants (yes, we’ve had requests), or anything that plugs into a gaming console. Sorry, Rohan.

Slide 3: The Fine Print
- Receipts *must* be uploaded to the research office’s portal within 30 days. No receipt? No stipend. No exceptions.
- Manager approval is *mandatory*. If your PI doesn’t sign off, you’re SOL.
- Hybrid workers: you’re eligible, but you can’t double-dip if you’ve already used the stipend for on-campus gear.

Slide 4: Pro Tips
- If you’re ordering lab equipment (looking at you, biology folks), that’s a *separate* budget. This stipend’s for *your* workspace, not your petri dishes.
- Need help? Ping Tatiana in the research office. She’s the queen of stipend approvals and also the only one who understands the portal’s ‘error code 404: humanity not found’ messages.

Slide 5: FAQs
Q: Can I use this for a second monitor?
A: Yes, but if you already have three, maybe reconsider your life choices.

Q: What if I move mid-stipend?
A: Tough luck. The stipend’s tied to your current role, not your future digs.

Q: Can I get a stipend for my cat’s ergonomic bed?
A: …No. But we *do* have a ‘pets of the research office’ Slack channel. Just saying.

SLIDE DECK: API Gateway Migration – Research Office Impact

--- Slide 1: Title ---
‘API Gateway Migration: Why Research Cares (And You Should Too)’
*Presented by: Meera Iyengar & Larissa Camargo*

--- Slide 2: The Problem ---
- Current setup: 12 legacy APIs, all talking to each other like it’s 2010. Slow. Clunky. Embarrassing.
- New gateway: Faster, scalier, and—here’s the kicker—*auditable*. (Yes, finally. The feds will weep with joy.)
- Catch: Some of our grant-tracking endpoints are *very* attached to the old system. Like, ‘refuses to leave the nest’ attached.

--- Slide 3: What’s Changing ---
- /grants/submit → Migrating Week 1 (Larissa’s team owns this one. Pray for her.)
- /compliance/reports → Week 2 (Meera’s ‘fun’ project). 
- /collab/partners → Week 3 (If we’re lucky. If not, Week ‘Whenever IT Stops Panicking’).
- Everything else: ‘We’ll cross that bridge when we burn it.’

--- Slide 4: Risks (aka ‘Reasons to Drink’) ---
- Data loss: Unlikely, but if it happens, we’re blaming the medical school’s ‘unique’ firewall rules.
- Downtime: 30 mins max per endpoint. (Ha. We all know it’ll be 2 hours.)
- User confusion: High. Faculty will *definitely* call the helpdesk to ask why their ‘perfectly good’ 2015 bookmark doesn’t work.

--- Slide 5: Action Items ---
- Research PIs: Test your integrations *before* we flip the switch. No, we won’t ‘just delay it.’
- IT: For the love of all things holy, *document the new auth tokens*. 
- Everyone: If you see Caio, buy him a coffee. He’s earned it.

--- Slide 6: Q&A ---
(Prepare for chaos.)

SLIDE DECK: API Gateway Migration – Research Office Impact

--- Slide 1: Title ---
‘API Gateway Migration: Why Research Cares (And You Should Too)’
*Presented by: Meera Iyengar & Larissa Camargo*

--- Slide 2: The Problem ---
- Current setup: 12 legacy APIs, all talking to each other like it’s 2010. Slow. Clunky. Embarrassing.
- New gateway: Faster, scalier, and—here’s the kicker—*auditable*. (Yes, finally. The feds will weep with joy.)
- Catch: Some of our grant-tracking endpoints are *very* attached to the old system. Like, ‘refuses to leave the nest’ attached.

--- Slide 3: What’s Changing ---
- /grants/submit → Migrating Week 1 (Larissa’s team owns this one. Pray for her.)
- /compliance/reports → Week 2 (Meera’s ‘fun’ project). 
- /collab/partners → Week 3 (If we’re lucky. If not, Week ‘Whenever IT Stops Panicking’).
- Everything else: ‘We’ll cross that bridge when we burn it.’

--- Slide 4: Risks (aka ‘Reasons to Drink’) ---
- Data loss: Unlikely, but if it happens, we’re blaming the medical school’s ‘unique’ firewall rules.
- Downtime: 30 mins max per endpoint. (Ha. We all know it’ll be 2 hours.)
- User confusion: High. Faculty will *definitely* call the helpdesk to ask why their ‘perfectly good’ 2015 bookmark doesn’t work.

--- Slide 5: Action Items ---
- Research PIs: Test your integrations *before* we flip the switch. No, we won’t ‘just delay it.’
- IT: For the love of all things holy, *document the new auth tokens*. 
- Everyone: If you see Caio, buy him a coffee. He’s earned it.

--- Slide 6: Q&A ---
(Prepare for chaos.)

"Slide five: Next steps," he concluded. "We’ll finalize the migration plan by next week and present it to the compliance team. Ananya, can you draft the risk assessment for the outdated media?"

textB:
Hey folks,

So, we’ve been getting a ton of questions about the remote work stipend policy—like, *a lot*—and I figured it was time to send out a quick recap so everyone’s on the same page. First off, yes, the university *is* still offering the stipend for home office setups, but there are a few new tweaks you should know about. For starters, the max payout’s been bumped up to $1,200 (yay!), but now you’ve gotta submit receipts *within 30 days* of purchase. No more of that ‘I’ll get to it later’ business—finance is cracking down.

Hey team, so we’re finally kicking off that API gateway migration we’ve been talking about for ages. Yeah, I know, I know—it’s been on the backburner forever, but with the new semester rolling in, we’ve got to get our act together. The old gateway’s been limping along, and honestly, it’s a miracle it hasn’t crapped out on us yet. So here’s the plan: we’re moving everything to the new Kong setup. Why Kong? Well, it’s got the plugins we need, it’s scalable, and—let’s be real—it’s not the clunky mess we’re currently dealing with. 

Ananya’s already spun up a test instance over on the dev cluster (shoutout to her for putting up with my late-night Slack pings). We’ll need to migrate the student-services APIs first since they’re the most critical—enrollment, financial aid, all that fun stuff. Facilities is next on the list because, let’s face it, if the HVAC system API goes down, we’ll have a mutiny on our hands. 

I’ve attached a rough timeline (yes, it’s color-coded, don’t judge me). Aiming to have Phase 1 done by the end of the month. If anyone sees a problem—or, heaven forbid, a better way to do this—speak up now. Last thing we need is to realize halfway through that we missed something obvious. 

Oh, and if anyone from registrar or procurement is lurking on this thread: we’ll need your input on the auth tokens. The new gateway’s pickier about that stuff, so we’ll have to reissue a few. 

Let’s sync up tomorrow at 2 for a quick stand-up. Bring coffee. 

—Gordon

"Slide one: *Remote Work Stipend Policy – Research Office Perspectives*," Meera Iyengar announced, clicking through her presentation. The room was packed with department heads, their attention fixed on the projector screen. "As some of you know, the research office has been fielding concerns from faculty about the adequacy of the current stipend. Today, I want to walk you through why this matters for our work—and our reputation."

She advanced to the next slide, a graph showing a sharp decline in on-campus lab usage. "Here’s the reality: since the policy was introduced, our medical annex labs have seen a 40% drop in in-person activity. That’s not because people aren’t working. It’s because they’re working from home. And if they’re working from home, they need the tools to do it effectively."

A hand shot up. Vikram Salian, from the registrar’s office, spoke up. "But Meera, the stipend’s supposed to be a flat rate. If we start making exceptions for research faculty, where does it end? The history department’s going to want book allowances next."

Meera didn’t flinch. "It doesn’t have to be exceptions. It can be a framework. Slide three: *Tiered Stipend Model*." The slide displayed three columns—main campus, medical annex, and liberal-arts satellite—each with a different stipend amount and a list of eligible expenses. "This isn’t about favoring one department over another. It’s about recognizing that different types of work have different needs."

"And the cost?" Vikram pressed. "Where’s the money coming from?"

Meera flipped to the next slide, a pie chart breaking down the university’s discretionary funds. "We’ve identified $250,000 in unallocated funds from last fiscal year. That’s enough to cover the increased stipends for the medical annex and satellite campus faculty for the next two years. After that, we’ll need to reassess—but by then, we’ll have data to show whether this improves retention and productivity."

There was a murmur of agreement around the room. Meera allowed herself a small smile. "And finally, slide six: *Next Steps*. We propose a pilot program starting next semester. IT will handle the tech support side, Procurement will negotiate the vendor discounts, and the research office will track outcomes. Questions?"

Vikram leaned back, arms crossed. "I still think it’s a slippery slope. But... I’ll reserve judgment until I see the pilot results."

"Alright, team, let’s get this on the record," Larissa Camargo said, her voice crisp as she called the procurement meeting to order. The Zoom call flickered briefly before stabilizing, revealing the faces of her colleagues scattered across the university’s three campuses. "Today’s agenda: the remote work stipend policy’s impact on our vendor contracts. Bev, you’re up first—how’s Sutro Campus Dining Group handling the shift?"

Bev Koepper adjusted her headset. "They’re not thrilled. Sutro’s been supplying office snacks and coffee for faculty lounges, but with more people working remotely, their on-campus sales have dropped 30%. They’re asking if we can redirect some of the stipend budget to bulk deliveries of coffee and snacks to faculty homes."

Larissa raised an eyebrow. "So they want us to turn stipends into a meal-per-diem situation? That’s not what this policy was designed for."

"I know, I know," Bev said, holding up her hands. "But they’re a long-term partner, and they’re hurting. If we don’t work with them, they might pull out of the medical annex entirely. And then who’s going to keep the med students caffeinated during all-nighters?"

Dale Rambow, who’d been quietly taking notes, spoke up. "What about the equipment vendors? Trellis Research Computing reached out last week. They’re offering a 15% discount on high-performance laptops if we commit to a bulk order for remote faculty. Could we fold that into the stipend policy as an optional add-on?"

Larissa leaned forward. "That’s... actually not a bad idea. If we can negotiate a university-wide discount, faculty could use part of their stipend to upgrade their hardware through an approved vendor. It keeps the money in our ecosystem and gives folks more flexibility."

"But what about equity?" Bev asked. "Not everyone needs a high-end laptop. The liberal-arts faculty might prefer to spend their stipend on books or a second monitor."

Larissa nodded. "Then we make it optional. The stipend stays cash, but we provide a list of pre-approved vendors and discounts for those who want to use it that way. And we document everything so Finance doesn’t come knocking."

*Dale*: Yeah, but then we’re back to square one with equity. If we do this for IT but not for Research, people are gonna cry foul.

Today, I want to walk you through why this matters for our work—and our reputation."

She advanced to the next slide, a graph showing a sharp decline in on-campus lab usage. "Here’s the reality: since the policy was introduced, our medical annex labs have seen a 40% drop in in-person activity. That’s not because people aren’t working. Meera didn’t flinch. "It doesn’t have to be exceptions. It can be a framework. Slide three: *Tiered Stipend Model*." The slide displayed three columns—main campus, medical annex, and liberal-arts satellite—each with a different stipend amount and a list of eligible expenses. "This isn’t about favoring one department over another. It’s about recognizing that different types of work have different needs."

"And the cost?" Vikram pressed. "Where’s the money coming from?"

Meera flipped to the next slide, a pie chart breaking down the university’s discretionary funds. "We’ve identified $250,000 in unallocated funds from last fiscal year. That’s enough to cover the increased stipends for the medical annex and satellite campus faculty for the next two years. After that, we’ll need to reassess—but by then, we’ll have data to show whether this improves retention and productivity."

There was a murmur of agreement around the room. Meera allowed herself a small smile. "And finally, slide six: *Next Steps*. We propose a pilot program starting next semester. IT will handle the tech support side, Procurement will negotiate the vendor discounts, and the research office will track outcomes. Questions?"

Vikram leaned back, arms crossed. "I still think it’s a slippery slope. But... I’ll reserve judgment until I see the pilot results."

Okay, so this is a scanned PDF of the *very* official-looking draft of the remote work stipend policy that Bev’s been circulating. It’s got all the legalese and fine print you’d expect, but I’ll spare you the jargon and give you the gist. 

First off, the stipend’s only for employees classified as ‘regular, non-temporary’—so no grad students, adjuncts, or temp workers. Bummer, I know. It’s also prorated if you’re only remote part-time, which, honestly, feels like a way to nickel-and-dime folks, but hey, I don’t make the rules. 

The big debate right now is whether to handle this as a taxable benefit or just straight-up payroll. Bev’s leaning toward taxable because, quote, ‘the IRS is not our friend in this scenario.’ If we go that route, employees would see the stipend on their W-2s, which means they’d owe taxes on it. Not ideal, but apparently the alternative is even messier. 

There’s also a whole section on ‘eligible expenses,’ which includes things like internet, office furniture, and even software subscriptions (as long as they’re work-related). But here’s the catch: you’ve got to submit receipts, and anything over $100 needs pre-approval. So if you’re eyeing that $1,200 Herman Miller chair, you’re out of luck unless you get sign-off first. 

Oh, and get this—there’s a clause about ‘clawbacks.’ If you leave the university within a year of getting the stipend, you might have to pay it back. Because, of course, we can’t just make things *easy*. 

Anyway, Bev’s got a redline version with about a hundred comments from Legal, so who knows what the final version’ll look like. Fingers crossed it doesn’t get watered down into oblivion.
